records.text: The field of artificial intelligence has a long history.
The recent pace of change in artificial intelligence is unprecedented.
Until about 2022, artificial intelligence appeared as a regular scientific field.
Until about 2022, artificial intelligence progress was gradual and stepwise.
ChatGPT arrived in late 2022.
An explosion of large language models (LLMs) occurred in spring 2023.
The previous picture of AI as a field with gradual stepwise progress was shattered by the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022 and the subsequent explosion of large language models in spring 2023.
On 14 March 2023, Google announced the integration of large language models into its workspace.
On 14 March 2023, Anthropic unveiled its Claude models.
On 14 March 2023, OpenAI announced GPT-4.
Three years ago, it was still plausible that the rapid AI progress was a temporary breakthrough.
AI progress has not slowed.
AI progress is accelerating.
Frontier labs now use their own models to improve their models, edging toward recursive self-improvement.
A 2018 book surveyed prominent researchers about the timeline for human-level AI.
Ray Kurzweil, in a 2018 survey, predicted that human-level AI would arrive by 2029.
Most surveyed researchers placed human-level AI around 50 years away.
We are living through a phase change in AI.
Very few people foresaw this phase change.
The dream of creating artificial beings is ancient.
Many religious traditions describe humans as artificial intelligences fashioned by a deity from clay or other substances.
Greek mythology includes Hephaestus’ android robots.
Talos was a giant bronze guardian in Greek mythology.
Talos defended Crete by hurling rocks at enemy ships.
Throwing rocks with accuracy turned out to be much easier to automate than recognising enemy ships.
Recognising enemy ships is a quintessential computer vision problem.
Recognising enemy ships remains a challenging computer vision problem.
Medieval and early-modern automata included a programmable calligrapher and draftsman built by Pierre Jaquet-Droz in the 18th century.
These automata were purely mechanical.
These automata showed early glimpses of programmability.
The first real mathematical thinking about artificial intelligence started in the 20th century.
Alan Turing’s 1950 essay "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" posed the question "Can machines think?".
The essay introduced the Turing test.
In the Turing test, a human judge converses in writing with a human and a machine.
The machine passes the Turing test if the judge cannot reliably tell which is which.
The Turing test is probabilistic.
A single run of the Turing test is meaningless.
In a single run, the judge could just guess with 50% success.
The machine must make the judge’s recognition rate indistinguishable from random chance over repeated trials.
The Turing test has survived the shifting goalposts that plagued other AI milestones.
When Deep Blue beat Kasparov at chess in 1997, the response was that chess doesn't count because it's just tree search.
When AlphaGo conquered Go, the goalposts moved again.
Nobody ever dismissed the Turing test as trivial.
Free-form natural language conversation can cover any domain.
The domains natural language conversation can cover include computer vision, 3D reasoning, and common sense.
To predict the next token in a text, a system must implicitly learn about the world.
Predicting the next token is the core task of modern language models.
Large language models continue to surprise with emergent capabilities.
The Turing test was convincingly passed only in 2025.
The Turing test reigned for 75 years before being passed.
Turing’s original formulation of the test required the machine to impersonate a woman.
In Turing's original formulation, a man also tried to impersonate a woman.
In Turing's original formulation, every participant had to pretend to be somebody else.
The positive, engineering-oriented field of artificial intelligence began in 1956.
The field began at the Dartmouth Summer Research Project.
The Dartmouth Summer Research Project was organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester.
The grant proposal for the Dartmouth workshop was astonishingly ambitious.
The proposal was for a 2-month study of artificial intelligence.
The proposal conjectured that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can simulate it.
The proposal stated an attempt to find how to make machines use natural languages.
The proposal stated an attempt to make machines form abstractions and concepts.
The proposal stated an attempt to make machines solve problems then reserved for humans.
The proposal stated an attempt to make machines improve themselves.
The Dartmouth workshop did not solve these problems in one summer.
The workshop established artificial intelligence as a research field.
Early successes of AI included Logic Theorist.
Logic Theorist was a theorem prover.
Logic Theorist re-proved much of Principia Mathematica.
Early successes also included the General Problem Solver.
These early successes fueled high expectations.
Optimism in AI waned when projects such as machine translation failed to deliver.
The 1970s became the first AI winter.
During the first AI winter, funding dried up.
During the first AI winter, only a handful of researchers persisted.
Those researchers mostly worked on expert systems.
MYCIN was an expert system.
MYCIN diagnosed blood infections using approximately 450 heuristic rules.
The central challenge of expert systems was combining rules that were fuzzy and overlapping.
The field learned that pure logic was not enough.
In the 1980s, neural networks re-emerged.
The re-emerged neural networks included convolutional nets and recurrent nets.
These neural networks were hampered by insufficient data and compute.
The deep learning revolution ignited in the mid-2000s.
The deep learning revolution was enabled by larger datasets thanks to the internet.
The deep learning revolution was enabled by faster hardware.
The deep learning revolution was enabled by the switch from CPUs to GPUs.
These factors made training deep networks practical.
Since the mid-2000s, neural methods have become the dominant paradigm across virtually all of machine learning.
A computer program learns with respect to a class of tasks T and a performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience.
This definition forces the point that learning requires a numerical performance measure.
The numerical performance measure is called a loss function.
Designing the right loss function is often half the battle in deep learning.
Minimising the loss function should produce the desired behaviour.
In supervised learning, the dataset consists of input-output pairs {(x_i, y_i)}.
The goal of supervised learning is to learn the conditional distribution p(y | x).
Classification is a typical supervised learning task where y is a discrete label.
Example of classification: distinguishing cat vs dog.
Regression is a typical supervised learning task where y is a continuous value.
Example of regression: temperature prediction.
The model must generalize beyond the training set.
The model must avoid overfitting.
Labelling data is often extremely expensive.
Labelling data is especially expensive for dense tasks like segmentation.
In unsupervised learning, no y is provided.
In unsupervised learning, the dataset is just {x_i}.
The goal of unsupervised learning is to find structure in p(x).
Dimensionality reduction (representation learning) is a form of unsupervised learning.
Dimensionality reduction maps a high-dimensional input into a compact vector that preserves essential information.
A 1-megapixel image corresponds to approximately 3x10^6 numbers.
An auto-encoder is a canonical deep-learning approach for dimensionality reduction.
In an auto-encoder, an encoder compresses x to a latent z.
In an auto-encoder, a decoder reconstructs \hat{x} from z.
The loss in an auto-encoder is ||\hat{x} - x||^2.
This loss forces z to be a meaningful, low-dimensional summary.
Clustering is a form of unsupervised learning.
Clustering partitions data into groups where within-cluster similarity is high and between-cluster similarity is low.
Clustering can be seen as an extreme of dimensionality reduction where the latent space is a finite set of labels.
In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment.
The agent receives rewards.
The agent learns a policy to maximize cumulative reward.
In reinforcement learning, no dataset exists upfront.
The agent generates its own experience.
Classic challenges in reinforcement learning include balancing exploration and exploitation.
Another classic challenge is credit assignment for earlier actions when a reward arrives only at the end.
Reinforcement learning is a separate world with its own techniques.
Reinforcement learning will not be a focus of this course.
Active learning is a paradigm where the model chooses which data to label next.
Semi-supervised learning is a paradigm where part of the data is labeled.
Learning to rank is a paradigm to produce an ordering.
Learning to rank is used for tasks like search results.
Bootstrapping is a paradigm where a model improves itself using its own predictions.
Machine learning is essentially applied probability theory.
The course will not require heavy measure-theoretic machinery like sigma-algebras or Borel sets.
The course will cover core intuitions about random variables, densities, and basic rules.
A discrete random variable is one where the probabilities of outcomes sum to 1.
A continuous random variable is characterized by a density p(x) >= 0 such that the integral of p(x) over its domain equals 1.
Joint probability p(x, y) is the probability of two events occurring together.
Marginalisation gives p(x) = sum over y of p(x, y) for discrete variables.
Marginalisation uses integrals in the continuous case.
Conditional probability satisfies p(x, y) = p(x|y) p(y) = p(y|x) p(x).
From this, p(x|y) = p(x, y)/p(y).
Bayes' theorem states p(y|x) = p(x|y) p(y) / p(x).
x and y are independent if p(x, y) = p(x) p(y).
If x and y are independent, then p(y|x) = p(y).
The conditional probability p(y|x) is the central object of supervised learning.
In Bayesian inference, D denotes the dataset (observed data).
In Bayesian inference, θ denotes model parameters (everything we want to learn, such as weights of a network or probability of heads).
Bayes' theorem for model parameters is p(θ|D) = p(D|θ) p(θ) / p(D).
Since p(D) does not depend on θ, the posterior is proportional to p(D|θ) p(θ).
The likelihood p(D|θ) is how probable the observed data is given a particular setting of the parameters.
The likelihood is the part that the model definition directly gives us.
The prior p(θ) is our belief about the parameters before seeing any data.
The posterior p(θ|D) is our updated belief after incorporating the data.
The evidence p(D) is the integral of p(D|θ) p(θ) over θ.
The evidence normalizes the posterior to integrate to 1.
Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation finds θ_ML = argmax_θ p(D|θ).
Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimation finds θ_MAP = argmax_θ p(θ|D) = argmax_θ p(D|θ) p(θ).
The denominator p(D) is irrelevant for maximization, so usually only the numerator is used.
A direct problem in probability is to compute the probability of an event given a fully specified model.
An example of a direct problem: given an urn with 10 balls, 3 black, what is the chance of drawing a black ball?
An inverse problem in probability is to infer hidden parameters from observed outcomes.
An example of an inverse problem: given a drawn black ball, which urn did it come from?
Inverse problems naturally require Bayes' rule.
Classical probability interprets p as a limiting frequency in infinitely repeated experiments.
Many real-world questions concern unique, unrepeatable events.
Examples of such questions: "Will Spain win the 2026 World Cup?" and "Will AGI take over by 2030?".
The Bayesian interpretation treats probabilities as degrees of belief.
The Bayesian interpretation obeys the same mathematical rules as the frequency interpretation.
Both the frequency and Bayesian viewpoints are valid.
Bayesian reasoning is often more natural for the kinds of problems machine learning solves.
In the biased coin example, θ = p(heads).
The dataset D consists of n heads and m tails.
The coin tosses are conditionally independent given θ.
Given θ, the likelihood is p(D|θ) = θ^n (1-θ)^m.
Maximizing this likelihood with respect to θ yields θ_ML = n/(n+m).
θ_ML = n/(n+m) is the intuitive number of heads divided by total tosses.
For large n+m, θ_ML converges to the true θ.
Suppose only one toss is performed and the result is tails.
Then the likelihood is p(D|θ) = 1-θ.
This likelihood has no interior maximum.
Without a constraint, θ_ML would be -∞.
With the constraint θ ∈ [0,1], θ_ML = 0.
This ML estimate implies the coin will always land tails.
This conclusion is absurd after a single trial.
The mathematics is correct; the missing element is a prior belief about the coin.
A prior is a distribution over θ reflecting beliefs before data.
A uniform prior p(θ)=1 on [0,1] can be used when there is no strong opinion.
With the uniform prior, the posterior (up to normalization) is p(θ|D) ∝ (1-θ).
After normalization, the posterior is p(θ|D) = 2(1-θ) for θ ∈ [0,1].
The MAP estimate with the uniform prior is still 0.
The flat prior does not shift the maximum.
A crucial difference appears when moving from parameter estimates to predictions.
The ultimate goal of learning is not the parameters θ themselves, but making predictions about future data.
For a new coin toss, we want p(heads | D).
The probability p(heads | D) is computed by averaging the likelihood over the posterior.
The formula is: p(heads | D) = ∫_0^1 p(heads | θ) p(θ | D) dθ = ∫_0^1 θ p(θ | D) dθ.
With the uniform prior and D consisting of a single tail, the integral ∫_0^1 θ p(θ | D) dθ gives 1/3, not 0.
More generally, after n heads and m tails under a uniform prior, one obtains p(heads | D) = (n+1)/(n+m+2).
This formula is known as Laplace’s rule of succession.
Laplace’s rule of succession is less extreme than the ML estimate when data is scarce.
Both Laplace’s rule of succession and the ML estimate converge as the number of observations grows.
Full Bayesian inference – keeping the entire posterior distribution and averaging over it – yields smoothed, more cautious predictions that automatically account for uncertainty in the parameters.
For a real coin, our intuition is not a uniform prior.
We expect a real coin to be approximately fair (a bell-shaped curve around 0.5).
If we used a truncated normal distribution as a prior, the posterior would be a product of an exponential and a polynomial – messy to work with analytically.
The key idea is to choose a prior whose functional form looks like the likelihood.
Choosing such a prior makes multiplication easy.
Choosing such a prior ensures the posterior stays in the same family.
Priors with these properties are called conjugate priors.
For Bernoulli trials (coin tosses), the conjugate family is the Beta distribution.
The Beta distribution is: p(θ | α, β) = θ^(α-1) (1-θ)^(β-1) / B(α,β), for θ ∈ [0,1].
α and β are hyperparameters that encode our prior belief.
α = 1, β = 1 gives the uniform distribution.
Larger equal values (e.g. α = β = 10) produce a peak at θ = 0.5, reflecting strong belief in fairness.
If we then observe n heads and m tails, the posterior is also a Beta distribution.
The posterior is: p(θ | D) = Beta(θ | α + n, β + m).
The update rule is simply adding the counts to the hyperparameters.
Bayesian updating with conjugate prior: start with prior Beta(α, β).
After seeing data, the posterior becomes Beta(α + n, β + m).
To incorporate further data D', just use this posterior as the new prior and add the new counts.
The conjugate prior framework naturally connects to regularisation in loss functions.
Taking logs, log p(θ | D) = log p(D | θ) + log p(θ) + constant.
The log-prior acts as a regulariser on the parameters.
If we have k categories instead of two (a multinomial distribution with parameters θ_1, ..., θ_k), the conjugate prior is the Dirichlet distribution.
The Dirichlet distribution is: p(θ | α) ∝ θ_1^(α_1-1) θ_2^(α_2-1) ... θ_k^(α_k-1).
The update for the Dirichlet is: p(θ | x, α) = Dirichlet(θ | α_1 + x_1, ..., α_k + x_k).
Machine learning is, at its core, probabilistic inference: we update our beliefs about model parameters θ given data D using Bayes’ theorem.
The main objects are the likelihood p(D|θ) (the model), the prior p(θ) (our initial belief), and the posterior p(θ|D) (the updated belief).
The two standard point estimates are maximum likelihood (θ_ML) and maximum a posteriori (θ_MAP).
In practice we rarely have infinite data, so the prior matters.
The rational way to make predictions is to average over the posterior, yielding the predictive distribution p(x|D) = ∫ p(x|θ) p(θ|D) dθ.

Choosing a prior from a conjugate family (like Beta for a coin, Dirichlet for multinomial) makes computation trivial: the posterior has the same form as the prior, with hyperparameters updated by simple addition.
These ideas (probabilistic inference, priors, posteriors, conjugate families) are the foundation of all machine learning.
Even when training neural networks with gradient descent, the loss functions we minimise are essentially negative log-posteriors.
Regularisation terms in these loss functions are implicit priors.
